problem: Object goal navigation methods mostly rely on frontier-based exploration, which only counts gain at the endpoint, ignores the camera view frustum and is confined to 2D. Learned semantic guidance is closed-set and cannot use contextual instructions, and online informative path planning had not been applied to tasks needing semantics and termination.
motivation: Semantic mapping has matured (Habitat ObjectNav success rose from 14% to 59%), so exploration planning and semantic guidance are now the bottleneck. LLM common sense can give open-vocabulary priors on where objects are, and IPP/NBV planners reason about view gains along whole paths in 3D.
key_idea: Adapt online informative path planning to object goal navigation by defining gain as the aggregated OOI probability from a Bayes-filtered 3D voxel probability map, combined with LLM-derived object-proximity priors and a termination-aware node evaluation.
insight: The ablations show every module contributes. Removing the Bayes filter causes the largest drop (SPL 0.34 to 0.28, success 0.54 to 0.45) through false terminations and missed low-confidence detections. Removing LLM guidance drops SPL to 0.31 (about 9% relative), because the robot wastes time inspecting irrelevant areas such as a bathroom when looking for a bed. Local SBP connections matter for narrow corridors (SPL 0.28 without them).
method: 3D object probability mapping: SAN open-vocabulary segmentation heatmaps are fused into voxels with a Bayes filter (equal priors) for the OOI and for common objects, reducing flicker and misclassification; the fusion range is 5 m in Habitat.

LLM semantic guidance: GPT-4 assigns each common object a proximity level to the OOI (certain/near/average/far). These are mapped to probabilities and used to compute an imagined probability p_img per viewpoint over its unknown voxels. The map can be reused for new OOIs and accepts context text.

Node gain and termination evaluation: ray tracing gives the visible voxels; gain G(n) sums the OOI probability for mapped voxels and p_img for unmapped ones, weighted by occupancy probability. Termination T(n) counts high-confidence OOI voxels within 1 m, and nodes above T_min (size-dependent) are terminating nodes.

Sampling-based IPP tree: RRT* over sampled viewpoints with yaw/pitch optimised, terminating nodes oriented to frame the object, travel orientation along the motion direction, and ESDF (Voxblox) traversability checks with collision spheres.
Local SBP node connection: an OMPL planner finds alternative local routes when the straight-line connection fails (for example L-shaped corridors), penalising the inverse of obstacle clearance.

Node selection: choose the terminating node with the best T/C if any exist, otherwise the node with the best gain-to-cost ratio G(P)/C(P). The robot looks down and around at the start to estimate its height, and maximises pitch movement while travelling.

setting.backbone: SAN open-vocabulary segmentation + GPT-4 (both frozen) with a classical RRT*-based IPP planner
setting.training_data: none (training-free, zero-shot; no training on the Habitat ObjectNav dataset)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D plus pose/state (ZED X RGB-D with SLAM pose on the real robot)
setting.action_space: continuous velocity (forward, turn, look up/down) in the Habitat 2023 challenge
setting.privileged: none (the 40 semantic labels for the common-object list come from the challenge spec; real-world common objects are manually selected)

numbers.extra: Habitat ObjectNav 2023 Challenge standard phase (1000 episodes); numbers printed as fractions
numbers.evidence: Table 1: Evaluation results on the Habitat ObjectNav 2023 Challenge (standard phase). IPPON (ours) 0.34 / 0.46 / 0.54

numbers_note: Values are printed as fractions (0.34), not percentages, and are copied as printed. The challenge standard phase is treated as the test split. Ablation rows are not listed separately. Real-robot result: 26/30 successes (0.87).
results: Zero-shot IPPON reaches SPL 0.34 and Soft SPL 0.46 on Habitat ObjectNav 2023, beating the best trained method SkillTron (0.28 / 0.36) by more than 20% relative, while its success (0.54) is below SkillTron (0.59). On the ANYmal robot it succeeded in 26 of 30 trials across 10 objects, including open-vocabulary and context-specific targets.
limitations: The list of common objects must be predefined, so objects that match no label can be misclassified and cause false terminations.
Mapping is object-level with no room-level distinction (a kitchen sink versus a bathroom sink), and very small objects such as a student card are hard to detect.
Real-robot evaluation is small (30 trials) and success is lower than the best trained method in simulation.
